3/1.about: A mournful, songlike lament in E-flat minor. A long, darkly coloured melody unfolds over a low, rolling accompaniment, rises to a passionate climax and then sinks back into resignation. It is one of the most intense of Rachmaninoff’s early miniatures, and it already shows his gift for long, singing lines and rich, sonorous writing for the piano.
3/1.ctx: The Élégie opens the five Morceaux de fantaisie, Op. 3, written in 1892, the year Rachmaninoff graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with the Great Gold Medal for his one-act opera Aleko. He was nineteen. The set was published in Moscow by Karl Gutheil in 1893 and dedicated to Anton Arensky, who had taught him harmony and composition.
facts: The first of the five Morceaux de fantaisie.

3/2.about: Rachmaninoff’s most famous piano piece is built on three massive, tolling chords — a descending motif marked fff — that open the work and return to close it. Between them comes an agitated central section of swirling triplets that builds to a thunderous climax, after which the opening chords return, spread across four staves for the fullest possible sonority. Its bell-like sound earned it the nickname ‘The Bells of Moscow’.
3/2.ctx: Rachmaninoff first played the prelude in Moscow in September 1892, soon after graduating, and sold it to Gutheil with the other Op. 3 pieces for a modest fee. Because Russia had not signed the international copyright agreements of the time, publishers abroad could print it freely, and it spread across Europe and America without earning him royalties. Audiences demanded it so relentlessly as an encore that he grew weary of it for the rest of his life.
facts: Rachmaninoff’s first major success, composed at just nineteen.
He grew to resent how often audiences demanded it as an encore.
Known popularly as the ’Bells of Moscow’.

3/3.about: A tender, lyrical piece in E major. The melody is sung in the tenor register, in the middle of the keyboard, while flowing chords surround it above and below — a texture that asks the pianist to project an inner voice through the accompaniment. Its warmth and unhurried breadth show the young composer’s gift for long-breathed melody.
3/3.ctx: Nearly fifty years after writing it, Rachmaninoff returned to this early piece in 1940, reworking its texture and harmony, and recorded the new version the same year. By then he was living in America, and the revision shows the older master refining a work of his student days.
facts: The third of the Morceaux de fantaisie.

3/4.about: A quick, capricious scherzo in F-sharp minor that portrays Polichinelle, the puppet clown of the commedia dell’arte. Brilliant leaping chords and cascading figures frame a gentler, more wistful middle section, as if the mask briefly slips to reveal the sad figure beneath. It demands agility, sharp rhythm and a strong sense of theatre.
3/4.ctx: Polichinelle is the French form of Pulcinella, the hook-nosed clown who became Punch in English puppet shows and was a favourite subject for artists of the late nineteenth century. Of the Op. 3 pieces it is the one most often played after the famous prelude, and pianists have long enjoyed it as an encore.
facts: Polichinelle is the French version of Punch.
The fourth of the Morceaux de fantaisie.
A showpiece of staccato and leaps.

3/5.about: A Spanish-flavoured serenade in B-flat minor, in which a strummed, guitar-like accompaniment supports a wistful, expressive melody. Graceful ornaments and sudden flashes of passion give it the character of a love song sung beneath a window.
3/5.ctx: The Sérénade closes the Morceaux de fantaisie. Its Spanish colouring reflects a taste for exotic settings shared by many Russian composers of the nineteenth century, from Glinka’s Spanish overtures to Rimsky-Korsakov’s Capriccio espagnol. Rachmaninoff kept the piece in his repertoire and revised it late in life, in 1940.
facts: The last of the Morceaux de fantaisie.

23/1.about: A quiet, brooding prelude in F-sharp minor that opens the set. A sombre melody unfolds over a restless, murmuring accompaniment, with inner voices weaving around it, and the music rises only briefly before sinking back into shadow. Its introspection sets a reflective tone for the larger, more brilliant preludes that follow.
23/1.ctx: The worldwide fame of his early Prelude in C-sharp minor may have encouraged Rachmaninoff to write more pieces of the kind. The ten preludes of Op. 23 date from 1901–03; only later, with the thirteen of Op. 32 in 1910, did they become part of a complete cycle of twenty-four preludes, one in every major and minor key, in the tradition of Bach and Chopin.

23/2.about: A majestic, virtuosic prelude in B-flat major. Sweeping figures surge up and down the keyboard in the left hand beneath powerful chords in the right, recalling in places Chopin’s ‘Revolutionary’ Étude, and a quieter central passage offers only a brief respite before the grand opening returns. It is a thrilling display of power and sonority.
23/2.ctx: Op. 23 is dedicated to Alexander Siloti, Rachmaninoff’s cousin, who had studied with Liszt and taught Rachmaninoff at the Moscow Conservatory. Siloti also championed his cousin’s music as a conductor and supported him financially through the lean years of depression at the end of the 1890s.

23/3.about: A dance-like prelude in D minor, marked Tempo di minuetto, with a sardonic, faintly sinister character. Its crisp, dry rhythms and spiky staccato chords give the old courtly dance a mocking edge, as if the minuet were being played by marionettes.
23/3.ctx: The preludes date from one of the happiest periods of Rachmaninoff’s life. In April 1902 he married his cousin Natalia Satina, whom he had known since childhood, after special permission was obtained for a marriage between cousins; the couple honeymooned in Venice, Vienna and Bayreuth.

23/4.about: A lyrical, nocturne-like prelude in D major. A long-breathed melody floats over a gently flowing accompaniment, gathering intensity as bell-like chords ring out above it, before subsiding into calm. It is one of the most tender and songful of Rachmaninoff’s preludes.
23/4.ctx: Its warm harmonies and broad melody are often compared to the Adagio of the Second Piano Concerto, completed only a short time before. The concerto’s success in 1901 restored Rachmaninoff’s confidence, and the Op. 23 preludes were among the first solo piano works to follow it.

23/5.about: One of Rachmaninoff’s most popular preludes, marked Alla marcia. A bold, martial theme in driving rhythm frames a broad, lyrical central section in which a singing melody floats over rippling accompaniment, before the march returns and vanishes in a quiet, surprising flourish. It combines sweeping Romantic melody with fierce rhythmic energy.
23/5.ctx: Written in 1901, the year of the Second Piano Concerto, this was the first of the Op. 23 preludes to be composed, two years before the rest of the set. Rachmaninoff played it often in his recitals, and it soon rivalled the Prelude in C-sharp minor in popularity; today it is the most frequently performed of the set.
facts: One of the most frequently performed of Rachmaninoff’s twenty-four preludes.
Composed in the productive years following the success of his Second Piano Concerto.
Marked ’Alla marcia’ for its bold, march-like character.

23/6.about: A tender, flowing prelude in E-flat major. A short, sighing melodic figure is repeated and varied throughout over a continuous, rippling accompaniment, creating a mood of quiet contentment. Its intimate warmth makes it one of the gentlest pieces Rachmaninoff wrote.
23/6.ctx: According to family tradition, Rachmaninoff wrote this prelude on the day his first daughter, Irina, was born in May 1903, which may account for its serene, happy character. It stands in strong contrast to the darker preludes around it.
facts: Built on repeated variations of a short melodic idea.

23/7.about: A restless, cascading prelude in C minor, marked Allegro. Torrents of rapid figuration pour through both hands, with a melody emerging from the rush, and the storm hardly pauses until the final bars. It demands great agility and evenness of touch.
23/7.ctx: Rachmaninoff was writing the Op. 23 preludes alongside his Variations on a Theme of Chopin, and both works reflect his fascination with Chopin’s legacy. Where many of Chopin’s preludes are fleeting sketches, however, Rachmaninoff’s are fully worked-out concert pieces written for a virtuoso.

23/8.about: A sparkling prelude in A-flat major, marked Allegro vivace. A warm, expressive melody sings through light, rippling right-hand figuration, giving the piece a shimmering, fountain-like texture reminiscent of Chopin’s études. It takes delicate control to keep the tune clear above the rapid notes.
23/8.ctx: Rachmaninoff introduced some of the Op. 23 preludes in Moscow in early 1903, and they were published by Gutheil later that year. The set confirmed his return to the front rank of Russian composers after the silence of the late 1890s.

23/9.about: A rapid, perpetual-motion prelude in E-flat minor, marked Presto. It is built largely on swirling double notes in the right hand over constantly shifting harmony, creating a blurred, whirlwind effect. It is one of the most technically demanding pieces in the set.
23/9.ctx: Its relentless double-note writing places it in the tradition of the virtuoso study, and it is often compared to Chopin’s Étude in thirds, Op. 25 No. 6. Rachmaninoff was one of the greatest pianists of his day, and the preludes reflect textures that came naturally to his exceptionally large hands.
facts: One of the most difficult of the set.

23/10.about: A quiet, contemplative prelude in G-flat major that ends the set in a mood of hushed reflection. A simple, gentle melody is enriched by warm, full harmonies and delicate inner voices, and the music moves unhurriedly towards a peaceful close.
23/10.ctx: After finishing these preludes, Rachmaninoff turned increasingly to conducting: from 1904 he spent two seasons at the Bolshoi Theatre, where his disciplined, precise work was widely admired. He would not write another prelude until the summer of 1910.

32/1.about: A brief, fiery opener in C major, marked Allegro vivace. Bold, brilliant gestures and restless rhythms sweep through its short span, and it ends as abruptly as it began, launching the set with a burst of energy.
32/1.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote all thirteen preludes of Op. 32 in a remarkable burst of creativity, in about two weeks in August and September 1910. They were published by Gutheil in 1911.
facts: The first of thirteen preludes in Op. 32.
One of the shortest of the set.

32/2.about: A gentle, lilting prelude in B-flat minor, marked Allegretto, in the rocking manner of a barcarolle. A wistful melody floats over the swaying rhythm, and the mood is quietly melancholy rather than tragic.
32/2.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed much of his music during the summer at Ivanovka, the Satin family estate in the Tambov province south-east of Moscow, which he managed in these years. Its peace and open landscape gave him the concentration he could not find during his busy concert seasons.

32/3.about: A vigorous, festive prelude in E major, marked Allegro vivace. Bold, ringing chords and dotted rhythms give it the character of a celebration, full of fanfares and pealing bells.
32/3.ctx: The Op. 32 preludes followed Rachmaninoff’s first American tour of 1909–10, for which he had written the Third Piano Concerto. Although he was offered tempting engagements in the United States, he returned home and spent the following summer composing.

32/4.about: A dramatic, wide-ranging prelude in E minor, marked Allegro con brio. Stormy, sweeping figures and march-like rhythms build to powerful climaxes, giving the music the scope of a small tone poem.
32/4.ctx: Earlier the same summer Rachmaninoff had completed his Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, his first major work for the Orthodox Church. The Op. 32 preludes show a similar concentration and a more austere harmonic language than those of Op. 23.

32/5.about: A serene, shimmering prelude in G major, marked Moderato. A delicate, birdsong-like melody drifts over a gently rippling accompaniment in the left hand, creating an atmosphere of stillness and light. It is one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved short pieces.
32/5.ctx: Its calm, open atmosphere is often compared to a summer landscape, and it is a rare moment of complete tranquillity in Rachmaninoff’s piano music. It has become one of the most frequently played of all his preludes, prized as much for the control of tone it demands as for its beauty.

32/6.about: A short, violent outburst in F minor, marked Allegro appassionato. Sharp, pounding rhythms and sudden flurries of notes give it the character of a furious explosion that burns itself out almost as soon as it begins.
32/6.ctx: One of the shortest pieces in the cycle, it shows how Rachmaninoff could compress intense drama into a very small space — a quality that links the Op. 32 preludes to the tighter, more concentrated style of his later music.

32/7.about: A lyrical, gently flowing prelude in F major, marked Moderato. A calm, songlike melody is gradually woven into a rich web of inner voices, and the mood is warm and quietly nostalgic.
32/7.ctx: Following the stormy F-minor prelude, it offers a gentle answer in the parallel major. Rachmaninoff arranged much of Op. 32 in such contrasting pairs — E major and E minor, F minor and F major, A minor and A major, B minor and B major — so that the set unfolds as a sequence of light and shade.

32/8.about: A restless, flickering prelude in A minor, marked Vivo. Light, quick figuration darts through the texture, and the music has a nervous, fleeting quality, like shadows passing by.
32/8.ctx: Rachmaninoff’s own playing was famed for its clarity, precise rhythm and lightness in fast passages as much as for its power. Pieces like this, with their rapid, feathery figuration, show that side of his pianism, in contrast to the grand sonorities of his better-known works.

32/9.about: A dreamy prelude in A major, marked Allegro moderato. Rippling triplet figures carry a warm, singing melody, and the music gradually swells and subsides in gentle waves.
32/9.ctx: It is one of the less often played preludes of Op. 32, overshadowed by the famous G-major and B-minor pieces, but pianists admire its warmth and the subtle way its melody grows out of the accompaniment.

32/10.about: A brooding, desolate prelude in B minor, marked Lento. A heavy, repeated rhythm and sombre chords create a sense of weariness, and a passionate central section builds to a tremendous climax of bell-like chords before the gloom returns.
32/10.ctx: Rachmaninoff considered it his favourite among his preludes. His friend the pianist Benno Moiseiwitsch said it was inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s painting ‘The Return’, which shows a man seated by a pond, looking towards his home — the same painter whose ‘Isle of the Dead’ inspired Rachmaninoff’s tone poem.

32/11.about: A delicate, rhythmic prelude in B major, marked Allegretto. Its light, dance-like figures and graceful turns give it a playful, almost whimsical character, and it passes by in a moment.
32/11.ctx: Placed between the tragic B-minor prelude and the restless G-sharp-minor, it acts as a brief interlude of lightness, its playful rhythms a deliberate relief from the intensity around it.

32/12.about: A restless, melancholy prelude in G-sharp minor. A shimmering, unbroken ripple of figuration in the right hand surrounds a wistful, folk-like melody in the left, and the mood is one of longing and unease. It is often considered one of the most beautiful of the twenty-four preludes.
32/12.ctx: Its mixture of glittering figuration and a simple, song-like tune has been compared to Russian folk song heard against the chime of distant bells. It is one of the most frequently performed of Op. 32 and a favourite choice for pianists who play just a few of the preludes.
facts: The twelfth of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32.
Composed at Ivanovka, the Rachmaninoff family’s country estate.
Regarded as one of the most lyrically beautiful of his preludes.

32/13.about: A grand, triumphant finale in D-flat major, marked Grave. It opens with solemn, hymn-like chords, gathers pace in a more agitated middle section and ends in a blaze of broad, ringing chords that bring the whole cycle to a majestic close.
32/13.ctx: D-flat major is the enharmonic equivalent of C-sharp, and this prelude is often heard as an answer to the famous Prelude in C-sharp minor, whose three-note motif it seems to recall in the major. With it Rachmaninoff completed his twenty-four preludes, eighteen years after the first.
facts: Closes the cycle of twenty-four preludes.
The last of thirteen preludes in Op. 32.

33.about: A set of études-tableaux, or ‘study-pictures’ — a genre Rachmaninoff invented, combining the technical challenges of a concert study with the vivid atmosphere of a character piece. Each is a self-contained scene, from brusque marches and whispering shadows to festive celebrations and tolling bells. Rachmaninoff never revealed the images behind most of them, believing listeners should paint their own.
33.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote nine études-tableaux at Ivanovka in August and September 1911, the summer after the Op. 32 preludes, but published only six of them in 1914. Two more appeared only after his death, and one was reworked for the later Op. 39 set. He explained his reticence by saying he did not believe in an artist who disclosed too much of his images.
parts: A sombre study, unpublished in his lifetime.
A study of sharp contrasts and brilliant figuration.
facts: Rachmaninoff refused to reveal what inspired them.
He wrote nine but published only six.
Ottorino Respighi orchestrated some of them in 1930.

33/1.about: A brusque, march-like study in F minor, marked Allegro non troppo. Heavy chords and a driving, dotted rhythm give it a determined, almost military character, with sudden contrasts of dynamics and texture along the way.
33/1.ctx: The study that opens the published set gives a taste of the new genre’s range: it demands power and rhythmic precision, but suggests a scene rather than a purely technical exercise. The études-tableaux mark a step towards the tighter, more rhythmic style of Rachmaninoff’s later music.
facts: The first of the Op. 33 études-tableaux.

33/2.about: A flowing, lyrical study in C major, marked Allegro. A long, singing melody floats over a continuous, rippling accompaniment, and the challenge lies in sustaining the line while keeping the figuration light and even.
33/2.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote these études in 1911, when he was also much in demand as a conductor in Moscow. Intimate, lyrical pieces such as this show the private side of his music behind the public career.

33/3.about: A sombre, slow study in C minor, marked Grave. Heavy, solemn chords and a dark, processional tread give it a funereal character, and the music unfolds with great gravity and restraint.
33/3.ctx: Rachmaninoff withheld this study from the 1914 edition, and it was published only in the late 1940s, after his death. Its material is thought to have been reused in the slow movement of the Fourth Piano Concerto, where a similar theme appears.
facts: Its material was later reused in the Fourth Piano Concerto.

33/4.about: A dark, march-tinged study in D minor, marked Moderato. Its brooding main theme moves with a heavy, deliberate tread, and the texture thickens as the piece builds, giving it a weighty, sombre character.
33/4.ctx: This is the other study Rachmaninoff left out of the published set; why he did so is not known. It remained unpublished in his lifetime and is still heard less often than its companions.

33/5.about: A rapid, whispering study in E-flat minor. After a brief, hesitant opening, quick, light figures rush past like shadows or gusts of wind, and the piece is over almost before it has begun. It demands a feather-light touch and great speed.
33/5.ctx: Its fleeting, atmospheric character shows how far the études-tableaux move beyond the traditional study: the technical challenge is there, but it serves a mood rather than display.

33/6.about: A festive, brilliant study in E-flat major, marked Allegro con fuoco. Ringing chords, fanfare-like figures and bustling rhythms create a scene of noisy celebration.
33/6.ctx: It is one of the few études-tableaux whose image Rachmaninoff revealed: in 1930 he told Ottorino Respighi, who was orchestrating several of them, that it depicted a scene at a fair. Respighi’s orchestral version brings out its colourful, crowded character.

33/7.about: A study of sharp contrasts in G minor, marked Moderato. A melancholy, singing theme alternates with brilliant, cascading figuration and sudden changes of mood, so that the piece seems to shift between memory and agitation.
33/7.ctx: The Op. 33 studies were published in 1914, three years after they were written — a delay typical of Rachmaninoff, who often reconsidered and revised his piano works before releasing them.

33/8.about: A dramatic study in C-sharp minor, marked Grave. A tolling, bell-like bass and imposing chords build to thunderous climaxes, and the piece closes the published set with solemn grandeur.
33/8.ctx: The sound of Russian church bells, which had fascinated Rachmaninoff since his childhood in Novgorod, echoes through much of his music, from the Prelude in C-sharp minor — in the same key as this study — to The Bells and the All-Night Vigil.

39.about: Nine large-scale study-pictures, denser, darker and more ambitious than the Op. 33 set. The harmony is sharper and more chromatic, the textures thicker, and the moods range from tempestuous drama and a stormy seascape to fairy-tale menace and a funeral procession, ending with a grand march. Together they form one of the summits of Rachmaninoff’s piano writing.
39.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the Op. 39 études in 1916–17, in the middle of the First World War and on the eve of the Revolution, and they were the last major works he composed before leaving Russia. Years later he shared the images behind several of them with Ottorino Respighi, who orchestrated five études-tableaux in 1930.
parts: A haunting seascape known as ‘The Sea and Seagulls’.
Little Red Riding Hood and the wolf.
facts: Rachmaninoff’s last piano works written in Russia.
Respighi orchestrated several of them in 1930.
No. 6 is a revision of a lost étude from Op. 33.

39/1.about: A stormy, turbulent study in C minor, marked Allegro agitato. Urgent, driving rhythms and swirling figuration surge through the piece, with heavy chords punctuating the torrent, making it a demanding test of stamina and control.
39/1.ctx: Rachmaninoff was deeply affected by the death of his former classmate Alexander Scriabin in April 1915, after which he gave recitals devoted to Scriabin’s piano music. Some writers hear an echo of Scriabin’s restless harmony in these études, whose language is more dissonant than anything Rachmaninoff had written before.

39/2.about: A haunting seascape in A minor, marked Lento assai. Slow, rocking figures suggest the heave of waves, and a plaintive melody drifts above them like distant cries, creating one of Rachmaninoff’s most atmospheric pieces. Its melody hints at the Dies irae chant that haunts so much of his music.
39/2.ctx: Rachmaninoff later told Respighi that this study depicted the sea and seagulls. It opens Respighi’s orchestral set of five études-tableaux, which was first performed in Boston under Serge Koussevitzky.
facts: Rachmaninoff shared the image with Respighi.

39/3.about: A driving, restless study in F-sharp minor, marked Allegro molto. Rapid, nervous figuration and cross-rhythms keep the music in constant motion, and the texture is lean and bristling rather than grand.
39/3.ctx: Rachmaninoff introduced the Op. 39 études in his own recitals in Petrograd and Moscow during the winter of 1916–17, some of the last concerts he played in his homeland.

39/4.about: A lively, humorous study in B minor, marked Allegro assai. Quick, playful figures and wry harmonic turns give it a sardonic wit, and the texture is light and transparent compared with its stormy neighbours.
39/4.ctx: Its lightness is a reminder that the Op. 39 set, for all its darkness, includes moments of humour and grotesque fantasy, in the tradition of Russian fairy-tale and character music by Mussorgsky and Rimsky-Korsakov.

39/5.about: One of the most passionate of all Rachmaninoff’s études-tableaux, marked Appassionato. A broad, surging melody is driven forward by an obsessive, pulsing accompaniment in chords, building to climaxes of overwhelming intensity before dying away in a hushed coda.
39/5.ctx: It is the best known of the Op. 39 études and a favourite of pianists and competitions alike, prized for its combination of lyrical sweep and physical power. Its turbulence is often heard as reflecting the anxious atmosphere of wartime Russia in which it was written.
facts: Composed shortly before Rachmaninoff permanently left Russia after the 1917 Revolution.
Marked ’Appassionato’ for its intense, driving character.
Rachmaninoff generally declined to explain the specific images behind his Étude-tableaux.

39/6.about: A quick, menacing study in A minor, marked Allegro. Growling, wolf-like figures in the bass alternate with scurrying, frightened runs in the treble, creating a vivid chase scene. It is often called ‘Little Red Riding Hood’.
39/6.ctx: The study began life as one of the Op. 33 études of 1911, which Rachmaninoff withheld and later revised for this set. He told Respighi it portrayed Little Red Riding Hood and the Wolf, and Respighi included it in his orchestral set.
facts: A revision of a lost earlier étude.

39/7.about: A grave, slow study in C minor, marked Lento lugubre. A heavy funeral-march rhythm, tolling bells and a sorrowful melody unfold in a long, overwhelming crescendo, before a hushed, chant-like close. It is the most solemn piece of the set.
39/7.ctx: Rachmaninoff described it to Respighi as a funeral march, with the singing of a choir, a fine, hopeless rain and the ringing of church bells. It is sometimes linked to the death of Scriabin in 1915, though Rachmaninoff never confirmed this.

39/8.about: A lyrical, flowing study in D minor, marked Allegro moderato. A warm, melancholy melody is set against rich, rippling accompaniment, and the mood is reflective and tender — a moment of calm before the grand finale.
39/8.ctx: After leaving Russia, Rachmaninoff devoted himself mainly to his career as a concert pianist, and his composing slowed dramatically. These études were his last original solo piano works for fourteen years, until the Variations on a Theme of Corelli in 1931.

39/9.about: A festive, march-like finale in D major, marked Tempo di marcia. Ringing chords, fanfares and pounding rhythms build to a brilliant, triumphant close, bringing the set to an end in grandeur.
39/9.ctx: Rachmaninoff told Respighi it depicted an oriental march. In December 1917, soon after the Revolution, he left Petrograd with his family on an invitation to give concerts in Scandinavia, and he never returned to Russia.

16/1.about: A long, songlike melody in B-flat minor unfolds over a rippling accompaniment, in the style of a nocturne. The mood is plaintive, and the tune keeps returning with ever more elaborate decoration, rising to a passionate climax before a quiet close.
16/1.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the six Moments musicaux in the autumn of 1896, partly out of financial need after money he was carrying was stolen on a train journey. The title recalls Schubert’s set of the same name, but Rachmaninoff’s pieces are much larger and more virtuosic.
facts: The first of six Moments musicaux.

16/2.about: A swirling, turbulent piece in E-flat minor. Restless, rushing figures churn beneath a sighing melody, creating a whirlwind of sound, and the music grows in intensity before fading away.
16/2.ctx: Rachmaninoff returned to this piece in 1940, more than forty years after its composition, and made a revised version. It is one of the most often played of the set, a favourite for its colourful, whirling textures.
facts: The second of six Moments musicaux.

16/3.about: A sombre, funereal piece in B minor, marked Andante cantabile. A solemn, chordal theme moves with the slow tread of a funeral march, and the music builds to an impressive, sonorous climax before fading into darkness.
16/3.ctx: The set is dedicated to Alexander Zatayevich, a friend and amateur musician who later became famous as a collector of Kazakh folk songs. This lament shows the Russian melancholy that runs through Rachmaninoff’s early piano works.
facts: The third of six Moments musicaux.
Has the character of a funeral march.

16/4.about: A stormy, virtuosic piece in E minor, marked Presto. Torrents of rapid figuration in the left hand drive beneath a bold, heroic theme in chords, and the music surges forward with relentless energy. It is one of the most demanding pieces in the set and a popular encore.
16/4.ctx: Its relentless energy recalls Chopin’s stormiest études, and it shows how far Rachmaninoff had moved from the salon style of his earlier miniatures towards a grander, more orchestral way of writing for the piano.
facts: The fourth of six Moments musicaux.
One of the most technically demanding of the set.

16/5.about: A calm, rocking barcarolle in D-flat major, marked Adagio sostenuto. A tender melody floats over a gently swaying accompaniment, and the mood is serene and dreamlike. It is among the most peaceful of Rachmaninoff’s early works.
16/5.ctx: Its calm offers a moment of repose before the grand finale, and it reflects Rachmaninoff’s love of the barcarolle, the Venetian boat song that Chopin, Tchaikovsky and others had made popular in piano music.
facts: The fifth of six Moments musicaux.
Written in the style of a barcarolle.

16/6.about: A grand, triumphant finale in C major, marked Maestoso. A stately theme rings out amid surging, full-toned figuration in both hands, and the music builds to a blaze of virtuosity that brings the set to a majestic close.
16/6.ctx: Written only a few months before the First Symphony’s premiere, this confident finale was among the last works Rachmaninoff completed before the crisis that would silence him as a composer for several years.
facts: The last of six Moments musicaux.
Ends the set in C major.

1.about: A youthful, brilliant concerto in F-sharp minor, full of energy, lyricism and virtuosity. It opens with a dramatic orchestral fanfare and a cascade of octaves from the soloist, followed by a tender, songful second theme. The short Andante is an intimate nocturne, and the finale sparkles with rhythmic vitality around a broad, lyrical central melody. The revised version of 1917 is leaner and more concentrated, and it is the one usually heard today.
1.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the concerto in 1890–91, at seventeen and eighteen, modelling its outer movements partly on Grieg’s concerto, which he admired. He played the first movement at a student concert in March 1892 with Vasily Safonov conducting, and dedicated the work to Alexander Siloti. In the autumn of 1917, as revolution broke out around him in Moscow, he revised it thoroughly, only weeks before leaving Russia for good.
parts: A bold opening leading into a lyrical main theme.

18.about: Rachmaninoff’s most beloved concerto opens with a series of tolling piano chords, growing from a whisper to a thunderous climax, before the orchestra launches the sweeping main theme. The Adagio sostenuto is a tender, dreamy nocturne in E major, its famous melody introduced by flute and clarinet over rippling piano figures. The finale combines dashing virtuosity with a broad, lyrical tune that returns in a triumphant close in C major. Its journey from darkness to light has made it one of the most popular concertos ever written.
18.ctx: The concerto marked Rachmaninoff’s return to composition after the failure of his First Symphony had left him depressed and unable to write. In 1900 he underwent a course of treatment with the physician Nikolai Dahl, who used hypnotic suggestion to restore his confidence, and he dedicated the concerto to Dahl in gratitude. The second and third movements were played first, in December 1900, and the complete work was premiered in Moscow in October 1901 with Rachmaninoff as soloist and Siloti conducting. Its melodies have since been borrowed for popular songs and films, most famously David Lean’s Brief Encounter (1945).
parts: Famous for its tolling opening piano chords leading into a passionate main theme.
A serene, deeply lyrical slow movement.
A vigorous finale that transforms its themes into a triumphant close.
facts: Dedicated to Dr. Nikolai Dahl, whose treatment helped Rachmaninoff overcome a severe creative block.
Marked his return to composing after the failed premiere of his First Symphony.
One of the most popular and frequently performed piano concertos ever written.

30.about: Known to pianists as ‘Rach 3’, this is one of the most formidable concertos in the repertoire. It opens with a simple, chant-like melody in octaves that Rachmaninoff said had simply written itself, and the first movement builds to an enormous cadenza — he wrote two, and the massive chordal alternative is now often preferred. The Intermezzo moves from wistful reverie to a flickering waltz and leads without a break into the finale, which recalls themes from the first movement and drives to a thunderous close.
30.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the concerto in the summer of 1909 at Ivanovka for his first American tour, practising the solo part on a silent keyboard during the Atlantic crossing. He gave the premiere in New York on 28 November 1909 with Walter Damrosch conducting, and played it again in January 1910 under Gustav Mahler, whose meticulous rehearsing impressed him. The dedicatee, Josef Hofmann, never played it in public, saying it was not for him. Its fearsome reputation was cemented by the 1996 film Shine, about the pianist David Helfgott.
parts: A famous, deceptively simple opening theme leading to enormous technical and emotional demands.
facts: Popularly nicknamed ’Rach 3’ for its extraordinary technical demands.
Its dedicatee, Josef Hofmann, reportedly never performed it publicly.
The subject of the 1996 film Shine, about pianist David Helfgott.

40.about: A restless, lean concerto in G minor, lighter in texture than its predecessors, with sharper themes and a wry, sometimes jazz-tinged modernity. The first movement launches straight into a sweeping theme over urgent orchestral chords. The Largo in C major is sombre and introspective, built on a three-note figure that resembles the nursery tune ‘Three Blind Mice’, and the finale is fast, rhythmic and full of sudden twists.
40.ctx: Rachmaninoff completed the concerto in 1926, drawing on sketches made years earlier, after nearly a decade in which exile and a busy concert career had left him almost no time to compose. The premiere in Philadelphia on 18 March 1927, with Leopold Stokowski conducting, was coolly received, and he cut and revised the work soon afterwards and again in 1941. It is dedicated to his friend Nikolai Medtner, who in turn dedicated his own Second Piano Concerto to Rachmaninoff.
facts: Premiered in Philadelphia with Stokowski conducting.

43.about: Twenty-four variations on the theme of Paganini’s Caprice No. 24 for solo violin. Unusually, the first variation comes before the theme itself, which is then played by the violins. The variations alternate brilliant display with deep lyricism, and several introduce the medieval Dies irae chant as a menacing counter-theme. The famous eighteenth variation turns Paganini’s theme upside down, slows it and sets it in D-flat major, creating one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved melodies.
43.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the Rhapsody in the summer of 1934 at the Villa Senar, the house he had built on Lake Lucerne in Switzerland, and gave the premiere in Baltimore on 7 November that year with the Philadelphia Orchestra under Leopold Stokowski. The same theme had already inspired variations by Liszt and Brahms. Rachmaninoff reportedly joked that the eighteenth variation was ‘for my agent’, and it has since appeared in many films, including Somewhere in Time (1980). In 1939 the choreographer Michel Fokine turned the work into the ballet Paganini.
facts: Its famous 18th variation inverts Paganini’s theme into a soaring new melody.
One of the last major works Rachmaninoff completed.
Quotes the medieval Dies irae chant, a recurring motif throughout his music.

28.about: A massive, dark sonata in D minor, in three large movements rich in themes and demanding in technique. Rachmaninoff originally conceived it with Goethe’s Faust in mind, and the movements can be heard as portraits of the restless Faust, the tender Gretchen and the demonic Mephistopheles, recalling Liszt’s Faust Symphony. The central Lento is a lyrical, song-like meditation, while the finale is a whirlwind of dense, driving virtuosity.
28.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the sonata in Dresden in 1906–07, where he had moved with his family to escape the distractions of Moscow, working on it alongside the Second Symphony. He called it wild and interminably long, and cut it substantially after consulting friends, among them the pianist Konstantin Igumnov, who gave the first performance in Moscow in October 1908. It remains one of his least performed major works.

36.about: A large-scale, densely virtuosic sonata in B-flat minor, in three linked movements. It opens with a cascading plunge down the keyboard into a heroic, bell-laden first movement; the central Non allegro – Lento is a wistful, melancholy song, and the finale is a brilliant, rhythmically driven Allegro molto that recalls earlier themes. Both the original version of 1913 and the shorter revision of 1931 are played today.
36.ctx: Rachmaninoff began the sonata in Rome in early 1913, while he was also working on The Bells, and completed it that summer at Ivanovka. In 1931 he revised it, cutting substantial passages and thinning the textures, feeling that the original had too much going on at once and was too long. Vladimir Horowitz later made his own version combining the two, with Rachmaninoff’s approval, and pianists remain divided over which best represents the composer.
parts: A turbulent, densely written opening movement.
facts: Rachmaninoff extensively revised the sonata in 1931, nearly two decades after its premiere.
Both the 1913 and 1931 versions remain in active use by performers today.
Composed in rooms in Rome once used by Tchaikovsky’s brother.

13.about: A dark, ambitious symphony in D minor, rich in thematic ideas and full of Russian character. Its four movements are linked by a motto theme derived from Orthodox chant and related to the Dies irae, which returns in varied forms throughout. After a restless scherzo and a tender, uneasy Larghetto, the finale erupts in a fierce, march-like Allegro con fuoco and ends with the motto hammered out by the full orchestra.
13.ctx: Rachmaninoff completed the symphony in 1895, and its premiere in St Petersburg on 28 March 1897, under Alexander Glazunov, was a disaster: the performance was poorly rehearsed, and César Cui wrote that if there were a conservatory in hell, the symphony would win its first prize. Crushed, Rachmaninoff withdrew it and fell into a long depression. The score was lost, but the orchestral parts were rediscovered in Leningrad in the 1940s, and the symphony was reconstructed and heard again in 1945. It is dedicated to Anna Lodyzhenskaya, a friend with whom he was infatuated.
parts: A slow introduction leading into a stormy Allegro.
facts: The disastrous premiere caused a creative crisis.
The score was lost and later reconstructed from orchestral parts.

27.about: A large-scale, richly melodic symphony in E minor. A brooding slow introduction gives rise to a passionate Allegro, followed by a brilliant scherzo with a fugal episode. The third movement, an extended Adagio, opens with one of the most famous clarinet solos in the orchestral repertoire and is built on some of Rachmaninoff’s most celebrated melodies. The festive finale gathers themes from the whole work into an exuberant close.
27.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the symphony in Dresden in 1906–07 and conducted its premiere in St Petersburg on 26 January 1908. Coming a decade after the failure of the First Symphony, its success was a personal vindication, and it won him the Glinka Award. For years it was usually performed with heavy cuts, until conductors such as André Previn championed the complete score in the 1970s. The Adagio’s melody was later adapted for Eric Carmen’s song ‘Never Gonna Fall in Love Again’.
parts: A brooding introduction leading to a sweeping main movement.
The symphony’s famous, richly melodic slow movement.
facts: Its slow movement contains one of Rachmaninoff’s most famous melodies.
Composed in Dresden, partly to escape his demanding Moscow concert schedule.
A triumphant success that helped heal the wounds of his earlier symphonic failure.

44.about: A nostalgic, rhythmically vital symphony in A minor, in three movements. A brooding motto theme, first heard on muted horn, clarinet and cello, returns throughout the work. The central movement combines a slow, lyrical Adagio with a quicksilver scherzo, and the finale is energetic and colourful, with a fugal passage and a quotation of the Dies irae. The orchestration is subtle and finely coloured, and the mood shifts between wistfulness and energy.
44.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the symphony in 1935–36 at his lakeside home in Switzerland; it was his first symphony in almost thirty years. The premiere in Philadelphia in November 1936, with Leopold Stokowski conducting, received a mixed reception, and he revised the work in 1938. Although it has never matched the popularity of the Second, many admirers regard it as his finest symphonic work.
parts: A motto theme opens the work.
Adagio ma non troppo – Allegro vivace
A slow movement with a quick scherzo at its heart.

45.about: Rachmaninoff’s last completed work, a three-movement orchestral suite of great colour and nostalgia. The first movement features a haunting alto saxophone solo and, near its end, quotes the main theme of his long-withdrawn First Symphony, transformed into a radiant major key. The second is a shadowy, melancholy waltz. The finale pits the Dies irae against a chant from his All-Night Vigil, ‘Blessed art Thou, O Lord’, and at its climax he wrote the word ‘Alliluya’ into the score — a passage often read as the composer’s farewell.
45.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the Symphonic Dances in 1940 at a rented summer home on Long Island, New York, and dedicated them to Eugene Ormandy and the Philadelphia Orchestra, who gave the premiere on 3 January 1941. He originally planned to call the movements ‘Noon’, ‘Twilight’ and ‘Midnight’, and hoped Michel Fokine would turn the music into a ballet, but Fokine died in 1942. At the end of the score Rachmaninoff wrote, ‘I thank Thee, Lord’.
parts: A nostalgic opening movement quoting Rachmaninoff’s own First Symphony.
A finale combining the Dies irae with a quotation from his own All-Night Vigil.
facts: Quotes his own First Symphony and his choral work All-Night Vigil.
Widely interpreted as the composer’s musical farewell.

29.about: An orchestral tone poem inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s painting, which shows a shrouded figure being rowed towards a rocky island of cypresses and tombs. The music is built on an irregular 5/8 metre, suggesting the slow, uneven strokes of the oars and the lapping of water. Out of this a passionate, yearning theme rises, often heard as a memory of life, before the mood darkens again and the boat’s rhythm returns, subsiding into a hushed, resigned close. The Dies irae chant is woven into the music.
29.ctx: Rachmaninoff saw a black-and-white reproduction of Böcklin’s painting in Paris in 1907 and composed the tone poem in Dresden in 1908–09, conducting its premiere in Moscow on 1 May 1909. When he later saw the original in colour, he said it did not move him and that, had he seen it first, he might never have written the piece. It became one of his most admired orchestral works during his lifetime.
facts: Inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s painting of the same name.
Rachmaninoff based it on a black-and-white photograph of the painting rather than the coloured original.
Written in an unusual 5/8 metre suggesting the rhythm of oars.

34/14.about: A wordless song for voice and piano, sung on a single vowel. One long, arching melodic line unfolds with extraordinary simplicity and emotional directness, rising gradually to a climax before a gentle close. Its warmth and melancholy have made it one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved melodies, and it is now heard in countless arrangements for cello, violin, orchestra and other instruments.
34/14.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the Vocalise in 1912 and revised it in 1915, adding it to his Fourteen Songs, Op. 34, as the final number. It is dedicated to the soprano Antonina Nezhdanova, who reportedly asked why he had written no words; he replied that her voice and artistry would express everything better than any text. He also made an orchestral version, which he recorded with the Philadelphia Orchestra in 1929.
34/14.sc: Voice and piano (or various instrumental arrangements)
facts: Sung entirely on a vowel sound, with no text.
Dedicated to the soprano Antonina Nezhdanova, who premiered it.
Now most often heard in one of its many instrumental arrangements.

42.about: Twenty variations on the old dance tune known as ‘La Folia’, which Corelli used in his Violin Sonata Op. 5 No. 12 and which Rachmaninoff mistakenly took to be Corelli’s own. The variations alternate brilliant virtuosity with passages of stark, austere beauty, and an Intermezzo and two lyrical variations in D-flat major provide contrast before the final variations storm to a climax and the work dies away quietly.
42.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the variations in the summer of 1931 in France, where he spent several summers at Clairefontaine, near Paris, before building his Swiss home. He dedicated them to his friend the violinist Fritz Kreisler. It was his last original work for solo piano. In a letter to Medtner he admitted that he sometimes skipped variations in concert when the audience began to cough, and that in one recital he played only ten.
facts: Based on the ‘La Folia’ theme long misattributed to Corelli.
Among the last solo piano works Rachmaninoff completed.
Written in his leaner, more concentrated later style.

22.about: Twenty-two variations on Chopin’s Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20, whose stately, chordal theme is first stated in its original form. The variations move from delicate ornament to stormy virtuosity, passing through a wide range of keys and moods before a grand, extended finale. It was Rachmaninoff’s first large-scale work for solo piano.
22.ctx: Rachmaninoff wrote the variations in 1902–03 and dedicated them to the celebrated teacher Theodor Leschetizky. He gave the premiere in Moscow in February 1903, and the work’s length and difficulty led him to mark several variations as optional cuts. It was the first of his three great sets of variations, followed by the Corelli Variations and the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini.
facts: Based on Chopin’s Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20.
Rachmaninoff’s first large-scale solo piano work.

19.about: A lyrical sonata in G minor in which the piano is an equal partner, with a richly written and demanding part. A brooding slow introduction leads to a passionate Allegro, and a restless scherzo follows. The Andante is a warm, song-like meditation often compared to the slow movement of the Second Piano Concerto, and the finale sweeps to a jubilant close in G major.
19.ctx: Rachmaninoff finished the sonata in November 1901, soon after the triumph of the Second Piano Concerto, and gave the premiere in Moscow in December with the cellist Anatoly Brandukov, its dedicatee. Brandukov was one of his closest friends and was best man at his wedding the following year.
parts: A slow introduction leads into the first theme.
facts: Dedicated to the cellist Anatoly Brandukov.
The piano part is unusually rich.
Completed shortly after the Second Piano Concerto.

9.ded: To the memory of a great artist (Tchaikovsky)
9.about: A grief-stricken piano trio in D minor, written in memory of Tchaikovsky. The long first movement grows from a sorrowful opening to intense climaxes, and the central movement is a set of variations on a theme from Rachmaninoff’s own tone poem The Rock, a work Tchaikovsky had admired. The finale ends in a funereal lament. The piano part is florid and dominant, almost like a concerto.
9.ctx: Rachmaninoff began the trio in October 1893, on hearing of Tchaikovsky’s sudden death, and finished it in December, inscribing it ‘to the memory of a great artist’ — an echo of Tchaikovsky’s own Piano Trio, written in memory of Nikolai Rubinstein with the same dedication. It was first performed in Moscow in January 1894 with Rachmaninoff at the piano, and he revised it in 1907 and 1917.
parts: A lament that builds to a passionate climax.
A set of variations on a plaintive theme.
A short, intense finale that recalls the lament.
facts: Dedicated ‘to the memory of a great artist’.

5.about: A suite of four poetic pictures for two pianos, also known as ‘Fantaisie-tableaux’, each prefaced by lines of poetry: a Venetian barcarolle, a night of love with the song of a nightingale, the falling of tears, and a jubilant Russian Easter. The two piano parts interweave richly, and the finale evokes the clamour of Easter bells around an Orthodox chant.
5.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the suite in the summer of 1893, when he was twenty, and dedicated it to Tchaikovsky, who had encouraged his early career. He gave the premiere with Pavel Pabst in Moscow in late November 1893, just weeks after Tchaikovsky’s death; Tchaikovsky had promised to attend. The epigraphs are by Lermontov, Byron, Tyutchev and Khomyakov.
parts: A warm nocturne of night and love.
A brilliant Easter finale with pealing bells.
facts: Each movement has a poetic epigraph.

17.about: A brilliant suite for two pianos in four movements: a stately, march-like Introduction, a glittering Valse, a tender Romance and a whirling Tarantelle. The two pianists are equal partners, and the music shares the sweep and warmth of the Second Piano Concerto, especially in the ardent Romance.
17.ctx: Composed in 1900–01, alongside the Second Piano Concerto, as Rachmaninoff was regaining his confidence as a composer, the suite was first performed in Moscow in November 1901 by Rachmaninoff and Siloti. It is dedicated to his friend the pianist Alexander Goldenweiser and has become one of the most popular works in the two-piano repertoire.
facts: Composed at the same time as the Second Piano Concerto.
The Tarantelle is a famous virtuoso finale.

37.ded: To the memory of Stepan Smolensky
37.about: A setting for unaccompanied mixed choir of the Russian Orthodox all-night vigil service, in fifteen movements. Rachmaninoff based ten of them on ancient chants and wrote the others freely in their style, creating rich, bell-like choral textures. The fifth movement, the Nunc dimittis, ends with a famous descent by the basses to a low B-flat.
37.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed the Vigil in less than two weeks in January and February 1915, during the First World War, and dedicated it to the memory of Stepan Smolensky, a scholar of Russian church music. The Moscow Synodal Choir gave the premiere in March 1915 with great success, but after the Revolution sacred music was suppressed in the Soviet Union and the work was rarely heard there for decades. Rachmaninoff asked for the Nunc dimittis to be sung at his funeral.
facts: Dedicated to the memory of Stepan Smolensky.
Contains a famously low part for basses.

35.ded: Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra
35.about: A choral symphony in four movements for soprano, tenor and baritone soloists, chorus and orchestra, on Edgar Allan Poe’s poem ‘The Bells’ in Konstantin Balmont’s free Russian translation. Each movement portrays a different kind of bell and a stage of life: silver sleigh bells for youth, golden wedding bells for love, brazen alarm bells for terror, and iron funeral bells for death. The orchestra imitates bells of every kind, and the work ends not in despair but in a quiet, consoling close.
35.ctx: Rachmaninoff composed The Bells in 1913 in Rome, in an apartment reportedly once used by Tchaikovsky, after receiving an anonymous letter suggesting Balmont’s poem; the sender later turned out to be a young cellist. He conducted the premiere in St Petersburg on 30 November 1913 and dedicated the work to Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra. He counted it among his favourites of his own works.
parts: Sleigh bells of youth and joy.
Golden bells of love and marriage.
Brazen bells of terror and fire.
Iron bells of death and silence.
35.sc: Soprano, tenor and baritone soloists, chorus and orchestra
facts: Based on Poe’s poem ‘The Bells’ in Balmont’s Russian version.
Dedicated to Willem Mengelberg and the Concertgebouw Orchestra.
Reputedly Rachmaninoff’s favourite of his own works.

21/5.about: A delicate song about lilacs at dawn, in which the poet goes out through the dewy grass to seek happiness among the flowers. The vocal line is gentle and unhurried, and the piano accompaniment shimmers quietly, like morning light through branches.
21/5.ctx: ‘Lilacs’ is the fifth of the Twelve Songs, Op. 21, which Rachmaninoff completed in 1902, the year of his marriage; the poem is by Ekaterina Beketova. He later made a piano transcription that he often played as an encore, and the flower became so associated with him that for years an anonymous admirer sent him bouquets of white lilacs after his concerts.
facts: Rachmaninoff made a piano transcription himself.
Sets a poem by Ekaterina Beketova.
One of twelve songs in Op. 21.

38/3.about: A charming song about daisies, in which the flowers are imagined as smiling faces dancing in the fields. The piano part sparkles with light, delicate figuration, and the vocal line has a graceful, floating quality.
38/3.ctx: ‘Daisies’ is the third of the Six Songs, Op. 38, composed in 1916 on poems by Russian Symbolist writers — in this case Igor Severyanin — and written for the soprano Nina Koshetz, with whom Rachmaninoff performed. They were the last songs he wrote. His later piano transcription has become a favourite recital piece.
facts: Sets a poem by Igor Severyanin.
One of six songs in Op. 38.

10/5.about: A playful, scherzo-like piece in G major, full of light, dancing staccato and delicate humour. Quick, capricious figures bounce between the hands around a gentler middle section, and the mood is bright and witty throughout.
10/5.ctx: The Humoresque is the fifth of the seven Morceaux de salon, Op. 10, which Rachmaninoff wrote in 1893–94, partly to earn a living as a young freelance musician. The set — a nocturne, waltz, barcarolle, melody, humoresque, romance and mazurka — reflects the fashion for elegant salon pieces, and Rachmaninoff returned to the Humoresque in 1940 to revise it.
facts: The fifth of seven Morceaux de salon.
Marked with a playful, scherzo character.
